finding: The live range of $220-$775 is about right. Built totals for the front axle (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Mazda3 2.0L about $191-$605 (0.6-1.5 hr); midsize 2012 Dodge Grand Caravan about $196-$596 (0.6-1.5 hr); truck 2016 F-150 about $353-$710 (1.0-1.5 hr); luxury 2015 Acura RDX about $244-$651 (0.7-1.5 hr). The live floor of $220 sits a little above our lowest totals ($191-$196), and those pair low-priced aftermarket parts bought online with a manufacturer warranty time, both less than a shop normally charges; AAA and KBB start at $250. The live top of $775 covers our highest total (truck with list-price Ford parts, about $710) with a little room. A European luxury car at a dealer, with genuine parts, wear sensors and a higher labor rate, can plausibly exceed $775; that case is not priced here. How solid the labor times are: every low end is now a stated time for the example vehicle itself. Three are manufacturer warranty times for exactly this job: Mazda's 0.6 hr to replace front pads and both discs on a 2014-2016 Mazda3, Chrysler's 0.6 hr to replace front pads and rotors on a 2011-2012 Grand Caravan, and Acura's 0.7 hr (discs plus pads, printed the same way in two separate bulletins) on a 2013-2015 RDX. The truck low end is a parts seller's 1-hour install estimate for the F-150, repeated on three of its front kits; the same seller prints 3 hours on a fourth, so its figures are loose. Warranty times are the bottom of what shops bill. Every high end is still the same single figure that is not for any example vehicle: a technician-run advice site's 1.5 hr (1.0 for pads plus 0.5 for rotors) on a 2019 Honda Odyssey, supported loosely by The Drive's 'an hour per axle'. Seized hardware, rust or caliper work will push real jobs past 1.5 hr. Confidence stays low because half of the hours figures (all four high ends) are not for the example vehicle; one vehicle-specific upper figure, such as a trade-press book time, would lift it. Not found: a manufacturer time for front pads and rotors alone on a full-size pickup (GM bulletin 22-NA-165 prints 2.1 hr for front and rear pads and rotors together on a 2023-2025 Silverado 1500, which cannot be split by axle; Ford, Toyota and BMW bulletins print none). The midsize example is a minivan from 2012 because that is the vehicle whose maker prints the time. Our totals sit below RepairPal's $574-$698; the gap is mostly parts (our low ends are online aftermarket prices of $119-$233, RepairPal's parts figure is $406-$452). No change to the live range is supported by this evidence.
extras: Quotes often add: brake hardware/clip kit and pad-wear sensors (European cars), brake fluid flush, caliper service or replacement if seized or leaking, rotor machining instead of replacement, shop supplies and disposal fees, inspection or diagnosis fee, and sales tax. The rear axle is priced separately.
